stops.name: Tirúa country, coast of Arauco, birthplace under the Nahuelbuta
stops.campa: A boy is born in the country of Tirúa, where the Nahuelbuta range walks down into the sea, son of the lonko Curiñancu. They name him Leftraru: the swift hawk, the traro that stoops faster than sight. The machis read the bird in him: a thing that circles high, watches long, and falls once. The land he opens his eyes on is the land the huincas have not yet touched; south of the Bío-Bío the rehues stand as they have stood since the world was ordered. He is born already belonging to the war that has not yet begun.

stops.name: Slopes of the Nahuelbuta cordillera, the boyhood
stops.campa: The boy grows in the mountain of the tigers, Nahuelbuta, among araucarias and mist. He learns what a lonko's son learns: the sling, the lance-play of the palin field, the memory-threads of lineage, the silence of the hunter. The elders say the hawk-child could stand a whole morning watching the condors work the wind, learning how a thing without weight defeats a thing with weight. North of the great river, in these same years, Pedro de Valdivia founds Santiago and writes to his King that there is no better land in the world. The two lives are already moving toward each other.

stops.name: Quilacura, before the Bío-Bío: the capture
stops.campa: Valdivia probes toward the Bío-Bío with sixty horse, and at Quilacura in the night the lances of the south meet Spanish cavalry for the first time. In the raids of these entradas the boy of Tirúa, some eleven years old, is taken. The canon is exact about the wound and vague about the day: a child roped among the yanaconas, marched north, away from the great river of his country, the frontier he will spend his whole life fighting back toward. The hawk is caged. The Spaniards do not know what they are carrying back to Santiago in their baggage-train.

stops.name: Santiago del Nuevo Extremo, Valdivia's stables
stops.campa: In Santiago the boy is given to the governor's own service: yanacona and groom, keeper of Pedro de Valdivia's horses. He carries water, oils leather, holds the stirrup of the conqueror of Chile. The Spaniards call him Felipe. But the stable is a school. He learns that the horse is not a monster but an animal that fears, tires, founders in soft ground; he learns its feeding, its shoeing, the number of leagues it can make and the hour at which it can make no more. The canon says it plainly: in the shadow of Valdivia, Lautaro studies Valdivia.

stops.name: Santiago, the school of war
stops.campa: Riding at his master's side on escort and muster, the page watches everything: how the harquebus is charged and how long it takes to charge again; how the cavalry forms and where a squadron of horse cannot go; how the Spaniards, so few, keep so many in obedience: by order, by terror, and by the horse. He learns Castilian and keeps Mapudungun beneath it like a knife under a cloak. The soldiers find the young groom quick, silent, useful. Valdivia trusts him near his person. The canon savors the irony: the conqueror himself is arming his destroyer, lesson by lesson.

stops.name: The road south, Valdivia's great entrada
stops.campa: Valdivia marches south with two hundred Spaniards and their yanaconas to conquer the country beyond the Itata, and the groom Felipe rides in his train, returning toward his own land in the enemy's livery. Every league is a lesson in logistics: the trains of pack-horses, the fords, the order of camp and sentinel. The boy who left Arauco roped in a baggage-train comes back watching the invading army from inside its own skin, counting its horses, measuring the exact width of its shadow. The Bío-Bío country rises around him like a memory returning blood to a numb limb.

stops.name: River Andalién, the night battle
stops.campa: By the Andalién, in the dark, Ainavillo hurls the massed levies of Arauco against Valdivia's camp, the first great battle of the war. The boy holds horses behind the line and hears his own people's war-cries for the first time since his capture; he sees them break at last against cavalry and shot, spears against powder. He sees also what the Spaniards do not see: that the squadrons came all at once, spent themselves in one wave, and had nothing behind. In the ashes of that night the whole military thought of Lautaro is quietly conceived: never again one wave.

stops.name: Fort of Penco, the mutilation of the prisoners
stops.campa: After the assault on the new fort at Penco is broken, Valdivia sits in judgment on his prisoners. The sentence is recorded by his own chronicler: hands and noses cut from some two hundred men of Arauco, the maimed sent home as living letters of the King's justice. The boy Felipe stands in the governor's service and watches the axe fall, and fall, and fall. The canon marks this day as the wound that never closes: what the Spaniards intend as terror, the hawk receives as instruction. He looks at the man whose stirrup he holds and finishes his studies.

stops.name: Concepción del Nuevo Extremo (Penco), the conqueror's new city
stops.campa: Valdivia founds Concepción on the bay of Penco, doorway to the conquest of the south, and the groom serves through its first raisings: palisade, church, the branding of encomiendas. Southward the new forts go up: Arauco, Tucapel, Purén, each a nail driven into the body of his homeland. Lautaro tends the horses of the men who ride out to collect tribute and rides among them, memorizing garrisons, distances, the seasons when the fords run low. The canon gives him these months as a spy given his commission by God: nothing he sees is wasted, and he sees everything.

stops.name: Out of the Spanish lines, the escape
stops.campa: On a day the chronicles do not fix (the canon says only that it came when he had learned all there was to learn), Felipe the groom vanishes from the Spanish service. A horse-boy missing; a matter for a shrug. He goes south through the fog country of Arauco, shedding the Spanish name on the trail like a snake's skin, carrying invisible contraband: cavalry drill, powder-times, the terror-economy of the conquest, the face of Valdivia. The hawk has slipped the jesses. Every Spaniard he passes on the road is a dead man who does not know it yet.

stops.name: Tirúa, the homecoming
stops.campa: He comes back to his father's hearth a man of eighteen who left as a child of eleven, speaking his own tongue with the ghost of Castile in it. Around the fires of Curiñancu's ruca he tells the country what he has brought: that the huinca dies like any man; that the horse is a servant that can change masters; that the thunder-weapon is slow between one thunder and the next; that the invincibility of the invader is a story the invader tells. The lonkos listen. The young men look at him the way men look at weather coming. Word travels along the coast: the hawk has returned knowing.

stops.name: Valley of Arauco, the great council
stops.campa: The lonkos of the sixteen ayllarehues gather in council, and the canon of the nation was written for this scene: the caciques quarrel over who shall bear the toqui's stone axe, until old Colocolo rises, 'ancient in years, and in wisdom more ancient,' the poem says, and turns their fury outward, ordaining the trial of the tree-trunk by which Caupolicán, who bears the log three days and nights, is raised toqui. And into that same order of war the returned hawk is received: Lautaro, who knows the enemy from inside, made lieutenant of the toqui, keeper of the new war. The assembly drinks and swears.
stops.quote: Caciques, del Estado defensores, / codicia de mandar no me convida / a pesarme de veros pretensores / de cosa que a mí tanto era debida; / porque, según mi edad, ya veis, señores, / que estoy al otro mundo de partida; / mas el amor que siempre os he mostrado / a bien aconsejaros me ha incitado.
stops.quote_source: Colocolo's speech, La Araucana, Canto II
